title: Quest of Dungeons
text: This game is essentially a remake of the 1991 Sega classic "Fatal Labyrinth", which is also available on Steam. Quest of Dungeons adds a few elements to the formula, some good and some bad, but doesn't really aspire to improve it so the few flaws that Fatal Labyrinth had are still here in Quest of Dungeons. This game adds more loot and a store to sell and buy items. But most of the loot is just junk to sell anyway, and there is nothing worth buying except healing potions. Quest of Dungeons also tries to add personality to the player character and the monsters, but fails completely. The character says random things like "This game was made with C++" and "This game was made with OpenGL". The monsters say equally weird things, according to another reviewer they are mostly references to movies that have nothing to do with the context of this game. Like in Fatal Labyrinth, the only way to heal between battles is to run around a bit. In this game the healing is a lot slower so the running around just to heal yourself gets even more tedious after a while. I quit playing soon after I got to the 4th floor of the dungeon. There you encounter monsters who steal stuff from your inventory. This is another "feature" that was present in Fatal Labyrinth as well. But again, Quest of Dungeons makes an annoying feature worse. In Fatal Labyrinth the monster sometimes stole an item from you, in this game they almost always succesfully steal from you, so you see the few good items you didn't sell before going to the 4th floor disappear from your inventory at an extremely frustrating rate. And you can't get stolen items back from the monster after killing it. Within a few minutes I lost the three keys I had in my inventory (the most important items in Quest of Dungeons and not easy to find) and the better part of my gold. This is such a cheap mechanism to make a game more difficult (and Quest of Dungeons has a few of those) that it made me decide to quit playing. Conclusion: the premise of the game is good but we saw that 25 years ago already in Fatal Labyrinth. And Fatal Labyrinth is still the better of the two games: it's longer, more balanced, less frustrating and annoying, it doesn't have the weird and even childish atmosphere and it has a "continue" system (if you play it via the emulator that comes with the Sega Megadrive Classics / Sega Genesis Classics collections, you can even save at any point). So I don't recommend this game but if you're looking to play a game just like it that doesn't have its flaws, I recommend Fatal Labyrinth instead.

title: Quest of Dungeons
text: Permadeath.  Get used it. Premise: Return the "light" stolen by a Dark Lord. Deceptively simple, easy, roguelike, single player, quest adventure.  Can be done in 30 minutes or less if you are good and lucky. Did I mention Permadeath? What makes this game a challenge beyond the randomly generated dungeons is Permadeath.  Each and every time you die the dungeon respawns and the player must begin again from the very beginning as a new character.  No in-game save points.  No tutorial.  Learn as one goes, and player arrogance and over confidence is the biggest enemy. 7 levels to traverse through with random encounters, traps, loot, side quests, and mini-bosses that will kick your butt. 4 difficulty settings: Easy, Normal, Hard and Hell.  For Hard and Hell all those OMG 'these are stupid tricks' come in handy when the monsters are OP and there is no shop keeper to buy health or mana from. Four character classes: warrior, wizard, shaman, and assassin each with their own unique play style and power ups (which one may or may not get during game play). Can you go the distance in this scoreboard game?  Simple things can be the hardest to achieve.

title: Quest of Dungeons
text: Although technically not a "roguelite", as it's TECHNICALLY a "proper" turn-based roguelike, this game probably more literally conforms to the other genre title than most... "The Orc and the Pie" is a joke about how, when you get down to it, the lazy standard of RPGs is to just say there's some monster that wants to kill you, and if you kill it, you get some random loot thing, and then get offered a chance to go kill another orc to get more pies.  Whoever made this game didn't get that it was supposed to be a joke. Play as one of four pre-defined stereotypes with no real character customization in a series of square rooms where you can either spam the ranged attack button (if a ranged attacker) or just ram directly into enemies until they all die. Then, once the orcs are dead, you get to run over anything in the room while spamming the "pick up" button, and occasionally run all the way back to a shopkeeper to empty out your pockets so you can carry more random crap. This game's version of pies are largely uninspired.  You have potions, "food" that are potions in disguise, armor and weapons that just straight give +damage or -damage with very few exceptions, and you'll largely be fighting enemies on floor 5 the exact same way as you did on floor 1.  In fact, you'll probably be fighting the SAME ENEMIES, too, since this game palette swaps all the enemies. Thanks to a lack of enough mana potions, if you play the mage, you'll be treated to a basic attack spell that takes 5 MP, enemies that take several bolts to kill, and needing to waste a dozen turns to get 2 MP back.  Enjoy the tactical depth of running in circles or smashing the wait turn button for hours to get your MP back after clearing a cramped room.  Since there's no hunger mechanics, you can waste infinite time, and are directly rewarded for doing so, with only the toll upon your own patience as a disincentive. Bosses may be tougher than you, but thanks to the I-take-a-turn-you-take-a-turn nature of the game, you can simply walk away from bosses to prolong combat as long as necessary for your passive regen to put you back up to full health while the bosses have no regeneration.  As a bonus, "poison" type effects keep working, so getting a single lucky fireball to start tapping away 3% health per turn and then kiting the boss across the whole dungeon is easy-peasy boss cheesing. Beyond that, everything in this game is either scenery or a target for vandalism.  It tries to add "humor" by having random quotes put out there like Dungeons of Dredmor did, but honestly, that just reminds me of how Dungeons of Dredmor is a much, much better game than this.  The "jokes" are even mostly recycled, and I can't even be bothered to stop to read them, after a while, much like I can't be bothered to stop to pick up the bajillion coins that fall out of the hundredth palette swapped rat I just barbecued with my thousandth fireball. Procedural content is only as interesting as the effort put into making each area actually feel different.  This game is just the same room copy-pasted every single time.  Kick in door, kill orc, take pie.  Kick in next door, kill orc, take pie.  Rinse and repeat until your eyes bleed.  Few games manage to be as offensively boring as this... In summary, don't play this game, it's a lazy knockoff Dungeons of Dredmor wannabe.  Play the real Dungeons of Dredmor.

title: Qvadriga
text: That's a great mobile or office game, one of the very best of them, but sadly it totally lacks any endgame content or storyline, or characters so it's not the best choice for PC gaming, still I've had enough of fun with it to recommend it to every turn-based strategy fan at least to try it out. Good realistic AI & carrieges' physics model along with 10 second real-time turns with pauses between them make it an ultimate gambling entertainment where you can simultaneously identify thyself with a brave rider, wealthy horse owner & an affectionate rooter. The gameplay is simple yet effective. You get gear: horses (speed & endurance), carriage (acceleration & endurance) & rider (turning skill & endurance), when they lose health their quality lowers so you want to get leading the race without losing too much of those resources. Every 10 seconds you have to make one decision - speed up or down, change lanes (1, 2 or 3 to each side), bash or whiplash rival moving at your side. You also get a random condition either good or bad which significantly changes your strategy. You can also bet on yourself. The whole point is to make money & become a prominent stabling. The Mediterranean region with lots of towns is at your service, every town has it's own hippodrome, their configurations & sizes are different, so you have to change your habits. When you become a champion at smaller arenas you can go to Rome, Constantinople or Alexandria to compete with the best & earn even more money - that's all, no logical game ending here. Still if you are fond of things like 'King of Dragon Pass' where your decisions are regularly put to the test of random outcomes & you can follow the mechanics of your triumphs & catastrophies in detail - you should by all means try out this small game with perfectly balanced risk-reward gameplay!

title: Qvadriga
text: I bought this game direct from the publisher before it was made available on Steam and lately I have transferred my license to Steam. This game is based very much on an old Roman chariot racing boardgame called Circus Maximus where you have to design your team and you then do a single race or a series of races. But this game adds more to that premise. For one thing the game introduces factions which all have their own concentrations, some build quality chariots, some have the best drivers other have tha fastest horses, there are quite a few of these traits that are introduced in the game which makes choosing your faction quite intriguing. Another thing the game adds is random events at the start of each race which might affect just you/someone else or everyone equally. For example you miught be prevented from whipping for the whole race which will penalise horse teams where endurance is high but speed is not. Also you might ahve a race where all the old wreackage is still on the track from the previous race making it far more deadly. Or you can be forced to start from a certain lane or have a rival in a race. These add loads of variety to each race. It also introduces faction leaders and leaderboards where each faction leader is ranked. You may make it you strategy to assassinate your faction leader in order to get your own best driver on the leaderboard adding extra strategy to the already packed with excitement races. You get many different authentic Roman and non-Roman race circuits from basic ones where you start off, up to the Circus Maximus, where you have to win three times to complete the game. As for the races themselves these follow the boardgame quite closely in that you can whip horses to make them go faster for a short time but this can damage them, you can try to whip other adjacent drivers or ram them or their horses, you can get damaged travelling over wreckage, you can be dragged and trampled to death etc etc. Its all very very Ben Hur in the most ruthless way possible. Of course though there is also a racing game in here and you can just try to win races through skill and speed. There is loads to enjoy in this game, I have to say I was very pleasantly surprised when I played it as to how much variety, strategy, and fun there is in here. Its probably one of my top twenty most favourite games of all time actually, and definitely one of the best purchases I have made over the last few years of gaming. Definitely recommended. And yes this concept would make a flaming wicked Nascar sort of game if converted! I remember playing  Grand Prix management game with this sort of overhead view and it was great. Someone has to make a modern racing game out of this!

text: Unpopular opinion I guess... but I really don't find this game anywhere near as fun as I hoped. For the most part the game is enjoyable, but some aspects feel cheap and repetitive. The biggest problem I have with the game is that the combat feels awkward and cheap (compared to other rogue-likes) for example you can be having a great run and then two large monsters spawn into an awkward locked room with you along with several knife throwing enemies, ruining your great run... and the worst aspect of it is you can come out of a difficult fight and get nothing but a few pieces of gold (which isn't massively useful). Which in binding of isaac terms that's like fighting the haunt on the first floor and getting Pageant Boy with only pennies as a return. Overall the game isn't bad but I feel in terms of a rogue-like it is disappointing.

title: Rampage Knights
text: For the price of admission imho this game doesn't offer much. You get to choose from 6 different classes (Adventurer, Barbarian, Pirate, Assassin, Warlock and Battle Mage), which are all suitable different: The Barbarian can't wear armor and is slow but tough, the pirate uses a cannon, the assassin can vanish, the battle mage uses spells instead of dodging, etc. This is all kinda nice. Unfortunately you have to unlock all the classes first. Now, granted, this is relatively easy, since you unlock casual mode, where you can simply restart a level, pretty early on (by just dying 3 times), but there's 1 achievement I still couldn't get to unlock the Warlock, because I never get ♥♥♥♥ing cursed or find a curse removal item. Because yes, this is a rogue-lite/like. After unlocking the characters there's not really any more progression. You do not get stronger after runs. You start just like that from the beginning. Going through the various levels takes about 1 1/2 hours to see the final boss...and then it's just rinse repeat with some random elements like traps, enemies and items of course. Since I've seen the same few weapons drop in the first 5 levels in pretty much every run, as well as the same items, I don't think there's too much variety here. Later on there are a few more, but it's no Isaac or anything like that. Items are armor, weapons, potions, scrolls, throwables and a kind of artifact you can find. Then there's various poisons, diseases and curses in the game as well. And you can definitely kill any chance of completing a run by picking up or using the wrong items. So far so semi-fun. Where the game falls apart imho is in the combat itself. It's slow, sluggish and very punishing. You think you hit an enemy but you're 1 mm short or the enemy swings a nanosecond earlier and you take damage. Damage you can't heal, unless you find healing potions. And you can die very fast to many of the enemies in the game, especially the giants. Evading, attacking, it's all not terrible, but not great either. However, in the later stages combat becomes terribly difficult to manage imho, because the game throws a lot of enemies on you and by that time you will also have some "familiars", little creatures that accompany you. On my first successful run I had like 6 or so floating around me, all doing their own little effects. Needless to say I killed stuff incredibly quickly, but I also didn't see my screen much in combat. I got this for like 3 bucks and I'm ok with that. It was fun for like 3 to 4 hours and now I'm done with it, since I'm not really interested in the other classes anymore after testing them out a bit. I only really liked the Barbarian and perhaps the Assassin. The battle mage cannot dodge, so he's a no go, despite having nice spells, the pirate can't do a charged attack, which is incredibly important to knock down groups of enemies imho, instead he gets a reloadable cannon that does no damage and only a little pushback...and like I said I haven't unlocked the Warlock, though he does sound interesting. Nice concept, terrible graphics, mediocre execution. Wait for deep sale imho.

text: This is an incredibly frustrating game. Unclear / unresponsive controls. You cannot initiate a new move before the other has finished. Sometimes moves work, sometimes they don't. Took me forever to figure out why my jump-slash wasn't working; it's because-- like a normal gamer-- I was still holding the jump key down when I initiated the attack. That's right-- the game doesn't let you hold down more than one key at a time without getting confused. So if you are halfway through executing an attack and realize it's not going to work, don't bother trying to dodge-- you have to wait for the animation to finish and the enemy is done pummeling you before you can do anything else. As with most rogue-likes, it's all about rolling broken loot that will carry you through to the end with little to no skill.

title: Rampage Knights
text: Remember ye olden days when you played games like Streets of Rage or Double Dragon? Rampage Knights is a beat 'em up game where you travel along slashing and bashing enemies and crushing them beneath your feet. Much like the aforementioned games, this is also a cooperative game. You can play it with friends online or with local shared/split screen. Along with the beat 'em up gameplay, it also has rogue-like elements to it. You go along through randomly generated areas and rooms, fighting against an array of enemies or having to avoid a fair many hazards. You can also gather items or spells along with equipping gear you might find to help you along the way. Along with these though, there are also diseases and curses which can hinder and harm you in different ways. The game is likely best played in multiplayer with a friend. You won't find any friendly fire happening (at least at Normal difficulty) so you won't have any issues in that department, but some curses can effect both you and your friend as you go along. Watch out though if your friend throws an explosive - or watch out for your friends when you throw them. Considering the strengths of the game, I wouldn't necessarily recommend it for its single player - but if you have a friend you are looking to play with, then a recommend picking it up the 2-pack on offer and playing it with them.

title: Reassembly
text: I see the appeal of this game, but once a-freaking-gain, it's a title that shipped long before it was finished. I LOVE these types of games. Build ship, gather resources, build bigger ship, smash enemies. That part of this game is fun. However, it's a broken PoS. Half the things don't work properly. List of broken stuff: -Drones fly off without reason into space and die. -Missle targeting flys around in circles for no reason. -Auto-target turrets don't auto-target 75% of the time. They sit there idling. -Auto-fire doesn't auto-fire when enemies are nearby 75% of the time. They sit there idling (noticing a pattern here?). -Ship re-building randomly doesn't work. Once, I was half-dead, went to allied territory and went to take a leak. Then I made a sandwich. Came back 5 minutes later and I still wasn't rebuilt. I had to exit and re-enter the game. -Sheilds randomly malfunction . No, there was not an EMP, the sheilds simply didn't want to turn on so I had to go kill myself to get them to work again (even though dying in this game isn't much of a consequence, it's still annoying!). -Thrusters on the side of the ship do jack-all. No matter what angle I put them at, strafing is a hundred times slower than going backward and forward. I put LITERALLY 10 times more thrusters on the sides of the ship than on the back of the ship, and no change. Barely any strafing at all. A thruster on the side of the ship does 1/100th the power of a thruster on the back/forward of the ship simply for the fact that it's on the side. I'm not sure if this is a glitch or if it's designed to be like that, either way, it's really damn annoying. -Half the time, the ship I'm currently flying either wants to go forward, or turn. Never both at the same time, but one or the other, exclusively. -Entering or exiting a menu resets the volume of the music to MAXIMUM. I play with my speakers pretty high up and turn most of the in-game volume down. This usually isn't a problem except in this game. Every time I go into the menu to change my ship, my fleet's ships, check the map, or pause the game, the volume for the music cranks all the way up to 100% for about a second, deafening me. This is more of a personal problem, but it's just another glitch that shows the game released too soon. -Every third game, my base spawns in the middle of god damned no where. No enemies within a hundred miles. Just dead, deep space between me and them. At the beginning of the game, you're especially weak, so you rely on your allies to help significantly, but it's impossible in these games, so the best advice I have is to just remake it. Another annoyance. -Every few minutes more I play this game I find another glitch/bug/thing I don't like. Positives: -Music is awesome. It gets my blood pumping at times and at others it makes me sit back and relax to the joys of the graphics. -Looks awesome. The graphics of this game are amazing. Beautifully done. -Ship building is simple, yet deceptively complex. You can't simply stick a massive shield on one side of the ship and have it work properly. You need to counter-balance it with another shield, or something with similar mass. Center of gravity of the ship actually matters and you can easily build a ship by accident that can only fly in circles. I love that! -Individual part destruction. When a part gets hit, you lose it, simple as that. If you lose your left aft engines, then guess what, you're flying in circles 'till it regenerates buddy. -Individual part regeneration. After a short period (dependant on the part), it regenerates, free of cost, without having to go back to a station to repair and refuel. -Unlock a part and you can use it as many times as you like. -Free ship re-design. Re-design your ship over and over and over aaaaaand oooooooveeeeeeer again all you want, it's free. You're gonna need those remakes to create a good one. You don't even have to enter a spaceport and whatnot. Once again, I'd love to love this game, I really would. There's a lot of great features and design aspects of the game I really love, but it's just not finished. It's just yet another game released before its time.
